title: Cantar de mio Cid
titleEn: The Song of the Cid — Both sides make ready for the meeting on the Tajo (tiradas 103–104, lines 1959–2012)
part: Tiradas 103–104 · Both sides make ready for the meeting on the Tajo (lines 1959–2012)
source: Ramón Menéndez Pidal (ed.), Poema de mio Cid, 2.ª edición corregida (Clásicos Castellanos 24; Madrid: Ediciones de “La Lectura”, 1923), pp. 252–255, lines 1959–2012 (tiradas 103–104). Text follows Pidal's critical text exactly, including its old accentuation and mixed spellings; Pidal's italics (his editorial restorations) are shown in [brackets], and a line he restores whole is flagged in its note. Line numbers are Pidal's. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed twelfth-century Castilian. Translations made fresh from the Old Spanish; Pidal's notes and vocabulary (1908–11) the lexical aids.

sentences.t:
Al rey ondrado delant le echaron las cartas;
quando las vío, de coraçón se paga:
sentences.l:
To-the king honoured before him they-cast the letters;
when them he-saw, from heart himself he-pays:
sentences.i: They laid the letters before the honoured king; when he saw them, he was glad with all his heart:
sentences.n: Tirada 103 (assonance á-a) — The king fixes the date for the meeting and makes ready with his men to go to it (Pidal: El rey fija plazo para las vistas. Dispónese con los suyos para ir a ellas). The line-ends cartas, paga, espada carry a stressed á with an unstressed a after it: a new assonance, a new tirada, after the ó of tirada 102. The letters are the Çid's, sent by two knights at the close of the previous part (v. 1957). Al rey ondrado … le, the king named with a and taken up again by le (compare a Minaya … los, v. 1894). delant, 'before, in front'. echaron, 'they cast, laid down'. se paga, from pagarse, 'to be pleased, satisfied' (pagado, v. 1922): the present after the preterites, the epic tense-mixing.

sentences.i: “Greet my Çid for me, he who in a good hour girded on his sword; let the meeting be three weeks from now. If I am alive, I shall be there without fail.”
sentences.n: Saludadme, imperative + me, 'greet for me'; a mio Çid, the person greeted marked with a. el que en buen[a] çinxo espada, the formula 'he who in a good hour girded on his sword', here without the word ora: buen[a], the a Pidal's (in italics), makes the adjective feminine, as if ora were understood. çinxo, preterite of çeñir, 'he girded'. sean, present subjunctive of ser, 'let (the meeting) be'. destas tres se[d]manas, 'of these three weeks', that is, three weeks hence; se[d]manas = semanas, the d Pidal's (in italics). The Çid has named the place, and the king now names the day, as Pidal's note to v. 1912 foresaw. s' = si, 'if', its vowel cut before yo. bivo so, 'I am alive' (so = soy). sin falla, 'without fail' (falla = falta), a stock filler (see v. 1968).

sentences.t:
Non lo detardan, a mio Çid se tornavan.
Della part e della pora las vistas se adobavan;
sentences.l:
Not it they-delay, to my Çid themselves they-were-returning.
From-that side and from-that for the meeting themselves they-were-readying;
sentences.i: They lost no time, and made their way back to my Çid. On this side and on that, they were making ready for the meeting;
sentences.n: The subject of the first verse is the two knights who brought the letters. detardar, 'to delay'; non lo detardan, 'they do not delay it'. se tornavan, imperfect beside the present detardan: the tense-mixing again. Pidal's note: della part e della, 'de una y de otra parte', 'on the one side and the other' (compare vv. 2079, 3139): the king's people and the Çid's both. pora = para. adobavan, from adobarse, 'to fit oneself out, make ready', the poem's word for gearing up (again at vv. 1986, 1997).

sentences.t:
¿quién vi[d]o por Castiella tanta mula preçiada,
e tanto palafré que bien anda,
cavallos gruessos e corredores sin falla,
sentences.l:
who saw through Castiella so-much mule prized,
and so-much palfrey that well goes,
horses stout and runners without fail,
sentences.i: who ever saw in Castile so many prized mules, so many palfreys of easy pace, war-horses stout and swift, without fail,
sentences.n: One long exclamation in the form of a question, opened by Pidal's ¿ and closed at v. 1971: 'who (ever) saw …?', meaning that no one ever did. vi[d]o = vio, 'saw', the d Pidal's (in italics). Castiella = Castilla. tanta mula preçiada, singular with tanta, 'so much prized mule', for 'so many'. mula, palafré, cavallo: Pidal's note to v. 1987 sorts them — the mule for baggage or, like the palafré, for the road; the cavallo for war. que bien anda, 'that goes well'. gruessos, 'stout, strong'; corredores, 'runners', swift. Pidal's note: sin falla, 'without fail', a filler (ripio) the poem shares with French epic (his p. 44, n. 2).

sentences.t:
tanto buen pendón meter en buenas astas,
escudos boclados con oro e con plata,
mantos e pielles e buenos çendales d' A[n]dria[n]dria?
sentences.l:
so-much good pennon to-set on good shafts,
shields bossed with gold and with silver,
mantles and furs and good sendals of A[n]dria[n]dria?
sentences.i: so many fine pennons fixed to good lance-shafts, shields bossed with gold and silver, mantles and furs and good sendal silks of Andros?
sentences.n: meter, 'to put, set', infinitive still hanging on vi[d]o: 'who saw so many pennons set on good shafts'. astas, 'shafts', of the lances that carry the pennons. Pidal's note: boclados con oro, 'con bloca de oro', 'with a boss of gold' (his p. 104): the boss is the raised metal at the centre of the shield. pielles, 'furs, pelts'. çendales, 'sendal', a fine silk. d' A[n]dria[n]dria: Pidal's note explains the name, not the doubled form. In earlier editions he had read A[lexán]dria (French epic speaks of 'soie Alexandrine', Alexandria being the market for these silks); Schultz-Gorra and Bertoni proposed keeping the manuscript's d'Adria as a misrendering of the French 'cendal d'Andre'; Crescini (1917) showed that Andros, one of the Cyclades, famous for its sendals, was called Andra, Andre and also Andria. Pidal's italic n's mark the letters he adds to the manuscript's Adria. Why the print gives the syllables twice (Andriandria) is not explained; it may be a misprint for Andria (the italic n of both halves is plain on the scan), and the reading is uncertain. We keep it as printed; 'Andros' in the translation follows his note.

sentences.t:
Conduchos largos el rey enbiar mandava
a las aguas de Tajo, o las vistas son aparejadas.
Con el rey atantas buenas conpañas.
sentences.l:
Provisions large the king to-send was-ordering
to the waters of Tajo, where the meeting is made-ready.
With the king so-many good companies.
sentences.i: The king gave orders for plentiful provisions to be sent to the waters of the Tajo, where the meeting is being prepared. With the king, so many good companies!
sentences.n: Pidal's note: conduchos largos, 'provisiones abundantes', 'abundant provisions' (compare v. 804); largo here is 'generous, plentiful', not 'long'. enbiar mandava, 'he ordered to send', the infinitive set before the verb that governs it. las aguas de Tajo, 'the waters of the Tajo', the river the Çid named at v. 1954. o, 'where' (= do, donde), as at v. 1948. son aparejadas, 'are made ready', ser + participle. The third verse has no verb: atantas = tantas, 'so many'; conpañas, 'companies, retinues'.

sentences.t:
Iffantes de Carrió[n] mucho alegres andan,
lo uno adebdan e lo otro pagavan;
commo ellos tenien, creçer les ya la gana[n]çia,
quantos quisiessen averes d' oro o de plata.
sentences.l:
Infantes of Carrió[n] much glad go,
the one they-go-into-debt and the other they-were-paying;
as they were-holding, to-grow to-them it-would the gai[n],
as-many they-might-wish goods of gold or of silver.
sentences.i: The Infantes of Carrión go about in high spirits; some things they buy on credit and some they paid for, for as they reckoned it, their gain would grow — as much wealth in gold and silver as they could wish.
sentences.n: Iffantes, so spelled here, Ifantes at v. 1981: Pidal prints both. Carrió[n], the n Pidal's (in italics); on an enlarged crop the ó looks roman, as the established text has it, though the print is not sharp enough to be sure. alegres andan, 'they go (about) glad', andar with an adjective for a state. lo uno … e lo otro, 'the one thing … and the other', 'some … some'. adebdan, 'they run into debt' (debda = deuda, 'debt'), present beside the imperfect pagavan. commo ellos tenien, 'as they held, as they reckoned' (tenien, imperfect of tener in -ie). creçer les ya, the split conditional: creçerié + les, 'it would grow for them', the pronoun lodged between infinitive and ending (ya = ía). gana[n]çia, 'gain, profit', the n Pidal's (in italics). quantos quisiessen averes, 'as many possessions as they might wish' (quisiessen, imperfect subjunctive of querer); averes, 'goods, wealth', the noun of aver. The poet shows what the Infantes want from the match: the Çid's money.

sentences.t:
El rey don Alfonso a priessa cavalgava,
cue[mdes] e podestades e muy grandes mesnadas.
Ifantes de Carrión lievan grandes conpañas.
sentences.l:
The king don Alfonso in haste was-riding,
co[unts] and potentates and very great households.
Infantes of Carrión take great companies.
sentences.i: King Alfonso was riding out in haste, with counts and governors and very great retinues. The Infantes of Carrión bring large companies.
sentences.n: a priessa, 'in haste' (= aprisa). The second verse names those with the king, without a verb. cue[mdes], 'counts' (cuende, the old form of conde), the mdes Pidal's (in italics). Pidal's note: the conde had been since Visigothic times the governor of a district, exercising there, as the king's delegate, military, judicial and economic powers; the podestades were ricos omnes (great nobles) holding an office below that of count, the government or tenure of a fortress, a city or a territory. mesnadas, 'households', a lord's armed following. lievan = llevan, 'they take, bring'.

sentences.i: With the king go men of León and Galician retinues, and the Castilian ones, I tell you, are past counting. They slacken the reins and make straight for the meeting.
sentences.n: leoneses, 'men of León', the king's other kingdom. Pidal's note: gallizianas, 'gallegas', 'Galician'. non son en cuenta, 'they are not in (the) count', the formula of v. 915 (there of the foot-soldiers): we take it as 'past counting', the Castilian retinues being too many to number; it could also mean that they are not reckoned in with the others. Pidal has no note, and the sense is uncertain. las castellanas, the mesnadas understood. sabet = sabed, 'know (ye)', the singer turning to his audience. sueltan las riendas, 'they let the reins go' (as at v. 10). Pidal's note: adeliñadas, 'encaminadas en derechura', 'set on a straight course'; it is feminine, agreeing with the mesnadas and conpañas. The tirada closes with the whole royal host on the road.

sentences.t:
Dentro en Valençia mio Çid el Campeador
non lo detarda, pora las vistas se adobó.
sentences.l:
Within in Valençia my Çid the Campeador
not it delays, for the meeting himself he-readied.
sentences.i: In Valencia, my Çid the Campeador lost no time, and made ready for the meeting.
sentences.n: Tirada 104 (assonance ó) — The Çid and his men make ready for the meeting and leave Valencia (Pidal's rubric: El Cid y los suyos se disponen para ir a las vistas. Parten de Valencia.—El rey y el Cid se avistan a orillas del Tajo.—Perdón solemne dado por el rey al Cid.—Convites.—El rey pide al Cid sus hijas para los infantes.—El Cid confía sus hijas al rey y éste las casa.—Las vistas acaban. Regalos del Cid a los que se despiden.—El rey entrega los infantes al Cid). This part takes the long tirada only as far as v. 2012, where the Çid sets out; the meeting on the Tajo, the pardon, the marriages and the rest of the rubric follow in the next part. The line-ends Campeador, adobó return to the stressed ó of tirada 102. Dentro en Valençia, 'within Valencia'. non lo detarda, 'does not delay it', the words used of the messengers at v. 1964; se adobó, 'made himself ready' (adobarse, v. 1965): present, then preterite.

sentences.t:
Tanta gruessa mula e tanto palafré de sazón,
tanta buena arma, e tanto buen cavallo corredor,
tanta buena capa e mantos e pelliçones;
chicos e grandes vestidos son de colores.
sentences.l:
So-much stout mule and so-much palfrey of season,
so-much good arm, and so-much good horse runner,
so-much good cape and mantles and fur-tunics;
small and great dressed are of colours.
sentences.i: So many sturdy mules and palfreys in their prime, so many fine weapons and good swift horses, so many fine capes and mantles and fur-lined tunics; great and small alike are dressed in colours.
sentences.n: An inventory without a verb, matching the king's at vv. 1966–1971: tanta/tanto with the singular, 'so many'. Pidal's note: the mula served for carrying or, like the palafré, for the road (v. 1548); the cavallo for war (compare vv. 2572, 3242). de sazón, 'in season', in prime condition. arma, 'arms, armour'. pelliçones, 'fur-lined tunics' (compare pelliza). chicos e grandes, 'small and great', every rank of the household. son vestidos de colores, 'are dressed in colours': rich dyed cloth, a sign of wealth.

sentences.t:
Minaya Álbar Fáñez e aquel Per Vermu[doz].
Martín Muñoz [el que mandó á Mont Mayor],
e Martín Antolínez, el Burgalés de pro,
sentences.l:
Minaya Álbar Fáñez and that Per Vermu[doz].
Martín Muñoz [he who commanded at Mont Mayor],
and Martín Antolínez, the Burgalese of worth,
sentences.i: Minaya Álvar Fáñez and Per Vermudoz, Martín Muñoz, who held command at Montemayor, and Martín Antolínez, the worthy man of Burgos,
sentences.n: A roll-call of the Çid's men begins, running on to v. 1996; its verb comes only at v. 1997 (estos se adoban). Pidal's margin prints the number 1990 beside the Minaya verse, but counting down from 1985 and back from 1995 (and his footnotes to vv. 1987 and 1993) puts it at 1991: the label is set one line low, and we number by the count. aquel Per Vermu[doz], 'that Per Vermudoz', a familiar 'that'; the doz Pidal's (in italics), as in tirada 102. Pidal ends the verse with a full stop though the list runs on. The whole second half of v. 1992, [el que mandó á Mont Mayor], is Pidal's restoration (in italics), not the manuscript's; mandó, 'commanded, governed'; Mont Mayor, Montemayor (the Portuguese town Pidal identifies at v. 738, where the same half-line is the manuscript's own); á, the preposition, accented in Pidal's print. 1992b is Pidal's own number. el Burgalés de pro, 'the Burgos man of worth' (pro, 'worth, profit').

sentences.t:
el obispo don Jero[me], coranado mejor,
Álbar Alvar[oz], e Alvar Sa[l]vadórez,
Muño Gustioz, el cavallero de pro,
Galind Garçiaz, el que f[o] de Aragón:
sentences.l:
the bishop don Jero[me], tonsured-one better,
Álbar Alvar[oz], and Alvar Sa[l]vadórez,
Muño Gustioz, the knight of worth,
Galind Garçiaz, he who w[as] from Aragón:
sentences.i: the bishop, Don Jerome, best of churchmen, Álvar Álvarez and Álvar Salvadórez, Muño Gustioz, the knight of worth, and Galín García, who was from Aragon:
sentences.n: Jero[me], the me Pidal's (in italics): the French cleric whom the Çid made bishop of Valencia. Pidal's note: coranado, 'clérigo', 'cleric' (compare v. 1501), so spelled here for coronado, 'the tonsured one'; mejor, 'best'. Alvar[oz], the oz Pidal's (in italics): Álvar Álvarez. Sa[l]vadórez, the l Pidal's (in italics); Pidal leaves the second Alvar unaccented. de pro, as at v. 1992b. Galind Garçiaz is the Galín Garcia[z] of vv. 443 and 740 (there el bueno de Aragón), Galín García in the translation as there; Pidal prints Galind here. f[o] = fue, 'was', the o Pidal's (in italics): 'he who was from Aragon'. The colon gathers the list for the verb that follows.

sentences.t:
estos se adoban por ir con el Campeador,
e todos los otros [quantos] que i son.
sentences.l:
these themselves ready for to-go with the Campeador,
and all the others [as-many] who there are.
sentences.i: these make ready to ride with the Campeador, and all the others, as many as are there.
sentences.n: se adoban, 'make themselves ready' (adobarse again). por ir, 'to go', por + infinitive of purpose. [quantos], Pidal's (in italics): quantos que i son, 'as many as are there', the que doubling quantos as it often does. i, 'there'.

sentences.t:
Álvar Salvadórez e Galind Garciaz el de Aragón,
a aquestos dos mandó el Campeador
que curien a Valencia d' alma e de corazón,
e todos los [otros] que en poder dessos fossen.
sentences.l:
Álvar Salvadórez and Galind Garciaz he of Aragón,
to these two ordered the Campeador
that they-guard to Valencia from soul and from heart,
and all the [others] who in power of-those might-be.
sentences.i: Álvar Salvadórez and Galín García of Aragon — these two the Campeador ordered to guard Valencia with all their heart and soul, and all the others who were in their keeping.
sentences.n: The two last named in the roll are now left behind: the verse names them first and a aquestos dos, 'to these two', takes them up again. Garciaz, Valencia and corazón are printed here without the cedilla, beside Garçiaz, Valençia and coraçón elsewhere; kept as Pidal prints them. 2000b is Pidal's own number. curien, present subjunctive of curiar, 'to guard, take care of'; a Valencia, the place marked with a like a person. d' alma e de corazón, 'with soul and heart', as at v. 1923. [otros], Pidal's (in italics). Pidal's note: en poder dessos, 'bajo la custodia de esos', 'in the keeping of those two' (compare v. 486): the others are those left in their charge, not further guards; dessos = de esos. fossen, imperfect subjunctive of ser.

sentences.t:
Las puertas del alcáç[er], [mio Çid lo mandó],
que non se abriessen de día nin de noch;
sentences.l:
The gates of-the citadel, [my Çid it ordered],
that not themselves should-open by day nor by night;
sentences.i: The gates of the citadel — my Çid gave the order — were not to be opened by day or by night;
sentences.n: Las puertas del alcáç[er] is set first and the sentence then changes course: 'the gates …, that they should not be opened'. alcáç[er], 'citadel, fortress' (from Arabic al-qaṣr), the er Pidal's (in italics). The whole second half of v. 2002, [mio Çid lo mandó], 'my Çid ordered it', is Pidal's restoration (in italics), not the manuscript's. non se abriessen, imperfect subjunctive with se: 'that they be not opened'. noch = noche.

sentences.i: inside are his wife and both his daughters, in whom his heart and soul are bound up, and other ladies who serve them to their liking;
sentences.n: dentro es, 'inside is': ser of place, singular before a plural subject. su mugier, Jimena (mugier = mujer). amas a dos, 'both the two', as at v. 1902. The number 2004b is ours: Pidal prints one more line between his margin labels 2000b and 2005 than his numbers allow, and the second line of this unit has no number of its own; the letter b is provisional. en que tiene su alma e s[o] coraçón, 'in whom he holds his soul and his heart'; s[o], the o Pidal's (in italics), so = su. dueñas, 'ladies (of the household)'. a su sabor, 'to their liking': the ladies serve the mother and daughters as they wish.

sentences.t:
recabdado ha, commo tan buen varón,
que del alcáç[e]r una salir non pu[o]de,
fata ques torne, el que en buen ora naçió.
sentences.l:
secured he-has, as so good man,
that from-the citadel one to-go-out not can,
until that-himself he-return, he who in good hour was-born.
sentences.i: Like the good man he is, he has made sure that not one of them may leave the citadel until he returns, he who was born in a good hour.
sentences.n: recabdado ha, 'he has secured, seen to it', perfect of recabdar, ha set after the participle. commo tan buen varón, 'as (befits) so good a man'. Pidal's note: 'que ninguna puede salir', 'that none can go out': una in a prohibitive sentence means 'none, not one'. alcáç[e]r, the e Pidal's (in italics). pu[o]de = puede, the o Pidal's (in italics): a present, 'can', as Pidal's paraphrase puede shows, not the preterite pudo. fata = hasta, 'until'; ques = que se; torne, present subjunctive, 'until he returns'. el que en buen ora naçió, 'he who was born in a good hour', the formula.

sentences.t: Salien de Valençia aguijan [a] espolón.
sentences.l: They-were-going-out from Valençia they-spur [at] spur.
sentences.i: They were riding out of Valencia; they spur hard.
sentences.n: Salien, imperfect of salir in -ie, beside the present aguijan: the two verbs stand side by side without a link. aguijar, 'to spur, urge on' (compare v. 10). [a], Pidal's (in italics): a espolón, 'at the spur', spurring hard.

sentences.t:
Tantos cavallos en diestro, gruessos e corredores,
mio Çid se los gañara, que non ge los dieran en don.
sentences.l:
So-many horses at right-hand, stout and runners,
my Çid himself them had-won, that not to-him them they-had-given in gift.
sentences.i: So many war-horses, stout and swift, were led along — and my Çid had won them himself; no one had made him a gift of them.
sentences.n: Pidal's note: cavallos en diestro, 'caballo de armas', 'war-horses' (compare v. 1548): diestro, 'right hand', the hand on which a charger is led until it is needed. The first verse has no verb; the second takes the horses up again with los. gañara, 'had won', pluperfect indicative in -ra (= había ganado); se, 'for himself'. ge los = se los, 'them to him' (ge before a third-person object pronoun, modern se). dieran, pluperfect again, 'they had (not) given'. en don, 'as a gift': the horses were won in war, not received.

sentences.t: Hyas va pora las vistas que con el rey paró.
sentences.l: Now-himself he-goes for the meeting which with the king he-set.
sentences.i: And so he is on his way to the meeting he had settled with the king.
sentences.n: Hyas = hya se, 'now he goes off': hya, a spelling of ya, with se glued on (our reading of the form). pora = para. Pidal's note: paró, 'convino, concertó', 'agreed, arranged' (compare v. 33). This part ends here, in the middle of tirada 104: the tirada and its ó assonance run on into the next part, where the king reaches the Tajo a day ahead of the Çid.
